notes: Scope limited to major battles of the Gallic Wars (58-50 BC) and the Civil War (49-45 BC); earlier propraetorship in Hispania Ulterior (61 BC) excluded for lack of battle-level data.

Scope limited to major set-piece battles/sieges of the Persian campaign (334-326 BC) with quantifiable troop/casualty estimates. Excludes the 335 BC Balkan campaign (destruction of Thebes), the Battle of the Persian Gate (330 BC, widely described by ancient and modern sources alike as costly but with no surviving casualty figure at all, not even a disputed one), most of the Sogdian guerrilla campaign beyond Cyropolis/Jaxartes, the Mallian campaign (326-325 BC, no quantifiable casualty figures found despite being well attested qualitatively), and the return march and death (323 BC). Alexander is universally regarded as undefeated in pitched battle -- every row here is a Win, unlike the mixed records of other generals in this dataset.

Scope limited to major battles/sieges personally commanded (or personally supreme-commanded) by Genghis Khan with quantifiable troop-strength estimates, spanning the 1204 unification wars through the final 1226 Western Xia campaign. Excludes the Battle of the Thirteen Sides/Koyiten (1201) and the Battle of Khalakhaljid Sands (1203, Genghis's one major personal defeat) for lack of any troop or casualty figures in available sources; excludes the 1213-1215 Siege of Zhongdu for the same reason despite Genghis's personal command throughout. Also excludes battles led by subordinates in Genghis's name rather than under his personal or supreme direction: the 1208 Battle of the Irtysh River (Jochi), the Battle of Parwan (1221, Shigi Qutuqu, a Mongol defeat), and the 1221 sieges of Merv, Nishapur, and Gurganj (Tolui/Jochi/Ogedei/Chagatai). A systemic sourcing gap distinct from the ancient generals in this dataset: unlike Roman/Greek historiography, which nearly always states some own-side casualty figure (however self-serving), Mongol-era primary sources (the Secret History of the Mongols, Persian chronicles like Juvaini and Rashid al-Din, the Chinese Yuan Shi) and the modern historiography built on them almost never quantify Mongol losses, only the (often much larger) toll inflicted on the enemy. Every own_casualties figure in this general's rows is therefore an order-of-magnitude estimate inferred from qualitative source language ('light', 'minimal') or a single specific anecdote (the Zhongxing flood), not a source-attested count -- flagged per-row and noted here as the softest-sourced field across this entire dataset, ancient or medieval.

Scope limited to major set-piece battles/sieges personally commanded by Saladin as Sultan, from the 1175 Battle of the Horns of Hama (his first major independent-command engagement after Nur ad-Din's 1174 death) through the 1192 Battle of Jaffa (the last major action before the Treaty of Jaffa truce; Saladin died in March 1193). Excludes the 1167 Battle of al-Babein, fought during Saladin's rise as Shirkuh's senior lieutenant in Egypt, since Shirkuh, not Saladin, held overall command. Also excludes several 1178-1184 engagements (Battle of Hama 1178, Battle of Marj Ayyun 1179, the Siege of Jacob's Ford 1179, the Battle of al-Fule 1183, the Battle of Belvoir/Le Forbelet 1182) for lack of any quantifiable troop-strength or casualty figure for Saladin's own side in available sources -- the same no-fabrication bar applied to Alexander's Persian Gate and Genghis's Khalakhaljid Sands elsewhere in this dataset. As with the Genghis Khan rows, several battles here (the Horns of Hama, the Siege of Jerusalem, the Siege of Tyre) have only a qualitative casualty description ('minimal', 'light'/'heavy') rather than a source-given count; those own_casualties/enemy_casualties figures are flagged per-row as order-of-magnitude placeholders, not source-derived numbers.

Scope limited to major pitched battles personally commanded by Frederick II of Prussia across the First Silesian War (1741-42), Second Silesian War (1744-45), and Seven Years' War (1756-63): 12 battles from Mollwitz (1741) through Torgau (1760). Excludes the Battle of Kesselsdorf (1745), which was fought and won by Leopold I of Anhalt-Dessau while Frederick's own army was elsewhere -- the same personal-command bar applied to Genghis Khan's and Saladin's rosters. Also excludes the War of the Bavarian Succession (1778-79), fought under Frederick's overall direction late in his reign but essentially bloodless (nicknamed the 'Potato War'), and the final two years of the Seven Years' War (1761-63), which settled into maneuver and attrition without another pitched battle of comparable scale to those listed. source_confidence is Medium rather than Low across this roster: 18th-century Prussian and Austrian muster rolls and campaign histories give figures that are considerably better corroborated than the ancient and medieval rosters elsewhere in this dataset, but real disagreement of several thousand troops still shows up between sources for the same battle (Mollwitz's Prussian strength alone is quoted anywhere from 16,000 to 23,000), so High confidence is not claimed. resource_backing_tier is set per-row rather than fixed for the whole career: it starts at 3 during the Silesian Wars, when Prussia fought Austria roughly one-on-one with a full treasury inherited from Frederick William I, drops to 2 once the Seven Years' War's full coalition (Austria, France, Russia, Sweden, most of the Empire) is arrayed against Prussia from 1756, and drops again to 1 for 1758-1760 (Zorndorf, Kunersdorf, Torgau), reflecting Prussia's well-documented manpower and treasury crisis in the war's final years, kept solvent largely by British subsidy rather than its own resource base.

Scope limited to 14 major set-piece battles personally commanded by Napoleon across the First Italian Campaign (1796-97), the Egyptian expedition (1798), the Marengo campaign (1800), and the imperial campaigns from Austerlitz (1805) through Waterloo (1815). tech_era_tier is set to 4, one above Frederick the Great and the other Early Modern roster entry, on the era ordering in the schema's ERAS tuple, but this is a closer call than the other roster boundaries: Napoleonic infantry and artillery are still flintlock muskets and smoothbore cannon with animal-powered logistics and no rail or telegraph, essentially the same weapons/logistics/communications basis as Frederick's Seven Years' War armies -- the real Napoleonic innovation was organizational (the corps system, mass conscription, forage-based rapid marching), not a jump in the schema's specific weapons/logistics/comms axis. Tier 4 is used anyway to keep the tier sequence monotonic with era order and to leave meaningful separation for the Industrial era (rifled muskets, railroads, telegraph -- a materially larger technology jump than Napoleonic-vs-Frederick) and WWII (mechanization, aircraft, radio) still to come on this roster; noted here since a case for tier 3 (matching Frederick) is equally defensible on the schema's own definition. resource_backing_tier is set per-row rather than fixed, tracking the rise and collapse of French state backing across the career: 2 during the resource-starved Directory-era Italian and Egyptian campaigns (the Army of Italy's chronic pay/supply shortages are well documented), 3 at Marengo as First Consul, 5 at the imperial peak (Austerlitz through Eylau), stepping down to 4 as the Peninsular War drains resources during Wagram and Borodino, 2 as the Empire collapses by Leipzig, and 1 for the isolated, hastily-raised Hundred Days army at Waterloo. The Battle of Jena (1806-10-14) row covers only Napoleon's own engagement against Hohenlohe, not the simultaneous Battle of Auerstedt fought the same day by Marshal Davout against the main Prussian army -- excluded as a subordinate-commanded action, the same personal-command bar used for Genghis Khan, Saladin, and Frederick's roster. Waterloo's opponent_general_id is recorded as Wellington, who held the defended position throughout, though Blucher's Prussian army was decisive to the battle's outcome; the schema has one opponent field per row and Wellington is the single commander most directly opposing Napoleon's own attacks. Net record is 11 wins (2 Rout-level and 2 Pyrrhic among them: Wagram and Borodino, the latter recorded as a Win with objective_secured=false since the tactical field-holding produced no strategic result) / 2 Rout-level losses (Leipzig, Waterloo) / 1 Draw (Eylau, held per modern historiography over French claims of holding the field as a win, the same treatment as Frederick's Zorndorf).

Scope limited to major battles/sieges personally commanded (or personally supreme-commanded) by Ulysses S. Grant from his first independent command at Belmont (1861) through Lee's surrender at Appomattox (1865): 15 rows. tech_era_tier is set to 4, the same tier as Napoleon Bonaparte, rather than a distinct value -- the schema's 1-5 tier scale cannot give each of the six ERAS its own value without a collision somewhere, and the schema's own tier-5 definition ('mechanised warfare with radio and rail') is a closer match to the WWII roster entry still to come than to the Civil War, which had rail and telegraph but no radio or mechanization; a real technological gap between Napoleonic muskets/animal logistics and Civil War rifled muskets/rail/telegraph exists and is not captured by this field, noted here in case Phase 7's sanity pass questions the flat tier. resource_backing_tier is set per-row, tracking the Union's real mobilization curve: 2 at Belmont (1861, a new volunteer army barely organized), 3 through the 1862 western campaigns (Fort Henry, Fort Donelson, Shiloh), 4 through the 1863 Vicksburg/Chattanooga campaigns as Northern industrial mobilization matured, and 5 from the 1864 Overland Campaign onward, when the Union was a state able to fully replace its losses -- the textbook case the schema's tier-5 definition describes. political_constraint_flag is true for Shiloh (the post-battle firestorm and calls for Grant's removal that Lincoln overrode) and for every 1864 battle from the Wilderness through Globe Tavern (well-documented pressure not to appear stalled or in retreat ahead of the November 1864 election), false again once Lincoln's re-election removed that specific pressure. Excludes several Vicksburg-campaign battles fought primarily by subordinate corps commanders rather than under Grant's direct battlefield direction (Port Gibson: McClernand; Raymond and Jackson: McPherson; Big Black River Bridge: McClernand) -- the same personal-command bar used to exclude Genghis Khan's, Saladin's, Frederick's, and Napoleon's subordinate-led battles elsewhere in this dataset. Also excludes the Battle of Corinth (1862), where Grant was department commander but Rosecrans held the field command and Grant was not present, a genuinely different case from the 1864 Overland Campaign battles (Wilderness, Spotsylvania, Cold Harbor, and the Petersburg rows below) where Grant, as general-in-chief, traveled with the Army of the Potomac and personally directed its overall strategy while George Meade remained its formal tactical commander -- treated here as Grant's battles on the same 'personally supreme-commanded' standard applied to Genghis Khan and Saladin, not excluded as subordinate-led. The nearly ten-month Siege of Petersburg (June 1864-April 1865) is broken into four separately-documented named battles (Second Battle of Petersburg, the Crater, Globe Tavern, Third Battle of Petersburg) rather than folded into one aggregate siege-level row, since each phase has its own distinct, better-sourced outcome and figures, matching the one-named-battle-per-row granularity used for every other general on this roster. Net record is 9 wins (4 Rout-level: Fort Donelson, Vicksburg, Chattanooga, Appomattox) / 3 losses (Cold Harbor, the Second Battle of Petersburg, the Crater, none of them Rout-level -- Grant's own army was checked or repulsed but never broke) / 3 draws (Belmont, the Wilderness, Spotsylvania). Fort Henry is the one row flagged as fought mostly by the Navy rather than Grant's own infantry; included rather than excluded since Grant was present and in overall command throughout, unlike the excluded subordinate-led battles above.

Scope limited to battles/operations where Zhukov personally held direct field command of a Front/Army Group, not battles where he served only as a Stavka coordinator/representative overseeing subordinate front commanders -- the same 'personally supreme-commanded' bar used for Genghis Khan, Saladin, Frederick's Kesselsdorf exclusion, Napoleon's Jena/Auerstedt split, and Grant elsewhere in this dataset. On this basis, the Battle of Stalingrad, the Battle of Kursk, and Operation Bagration are excluded: Zhukov coordinated/planned these as Deputy Supreme Commander while named front commanders (Yeremenko/Rokossovsky/Vatutin at Stalingrad; Vatutin/Rokossovsky at Kursk; Rokossovsky commanding 1st Belorussian Front for the whole of Bagration) held direct command. The Leningrad Front command (9/14 Sept-27 Oct 1941, a genuine personal command) is also excluded, but for the opposite reason used for Alexander's Persian Gate and Genghis's Khalakhaljid Sands elsewhere in this dataset: despite a dedicated search, no source was found giving any quantifiable own/enemy troop-strength or casualty figure isolated to that specific five-week window (the one figure located, for the Sinyavino offensive he personally directed within it, has no numbers at all in any source, including Wikipedia's own unsourced page on it) -- the weakest-sourced gap in this entire dataset, ancient generals included. The First Rzhev-Vyazma Offensive (Jan-Apr 1942, personally commanded, Western Front) is likewise excluded for lack of any enemy-side (German 9th Army) troop-strength or casualty figure isolated to that specific operation, as opposed to the broader multi-year Rzhev campaign total or the separate, non-Zhukov-commanded Toropets-Kholm offensive that created the salient. The Battle of Berlin (April-May 1945 city-assault operation) is excluded as a separate row from the roster's Battle of Seelow Heights for the same overlapping-dates/double-counting reason documented on that row -- Seelow was Zhukov's own front's opening battle of the same operation, and Berlin's only available figures are an undifferentiated three-marshal combined total for the same period. tech_era_tier=5 for every row -- the first general in this dataset to reach the schema's top tier ('mechanised warfare with radio and rail'), a deliberate step up from Napoleon/Grant's tier 4, since the Eastern Front genuinely combined tanks, radio-coordinated combined-arms formations, and rail logistics at a scale the American Civil War (rail and telegraph, no radio or mechanization) did not reach. Net roster is 5 wins (2 Rout-level: Khalkhin Gol, Vistula-Oder) and 1 loss (Operation Mars, Zhukov's own best-documented personal defeat) across a 6-battle roster -- smaller than every other general in this dataset (range 8-15 elsewhere) despite an extensive search for additional candidates, a direct, structural consequence of the Red Army's Stavka command system routinely putting multiple named front commanders under a single coordinating deputy for the war's largest, most-quantified operations (exactly the operations excluded above); this is flagged here rather than papered over by loosening the personal-command bar just for Zhukov.

Scope limited to major set-piece battles Hannibal personally commanded during the Second Punic War (218-202 BC) with quantifiable troop-strength and casualty figures on both sides. Excludes the 219 BC Siege of Saguntum (the war's opening action) and the 220 BC Battle of the Tagus against the Carpetani coalition -- both well-attested qualitatively (Saguntum's garrison 'nearly the whole fighting force was killed'; Tagus routed 'more than one hundred thousand' per Polybius) but with no quantifiable troop-strength or casualty figure for either side surviving in any source, the same no-fabrication bar applied to Alexander's Persian Gate and Genghis's Khalakhaljid Sands. Also excludes the three Battles of Nola (216, 215, 214 BC) and the Battle of Numistro (210 BC) for the same reason -- Livy himself hedges his own casualty claim for the first Nola battle ('I would hardly venture to assert...that 2,800 of the enemy were killed') and gives no troop-strength figure at all for any of the four -- and the Battles of Herdonia (212 and 210 BC), the Battle of Canusium/Asculum (209 BC), the Battle of the Silarus (212 BC), the Battle of Grumentum (207 BC), the Battles of Kroton (204-203 BC), and the Battle of Ager Falernus (217 BC), despite each having a hard Roman-side casualty figure (Herdonia I: 16,000 Roman dead; Herdonia II: 7,000-13,000; Canusium: 5,700; Silarus: 15,000; Grumentum: 8,000 Roman claim), because Hannibal's own troop strength is explicitly 'unknown' (Wikipedia's own infobox language) or given only as a partial detachment figure in every one of these, not a defensible total under his command at the battle. This pattern -- Roman chroniclers meticulously counting their own dead while rarely quantifying Carthaginian-side numbers for the long stalemate years after Cannae -- is a real and notable feature of the Second Punic War's surviving sources, not a research shortcut; it leaves this roster at 7 battles, short of the 8-15 range otherwise used in this dataset, the same kind of documented shortfall as Zhukov's 6-battle roster elsewhere in this file. Two included rows (Ticinus, Battle of Capua 212 BC) still have a real gap in one numeric field: Ticinus's casualties are only ever described qualitatively ('Light'/'Heavy') in sources, and Capua's own_casualties has no figure at all ('Unknown'); both are flagged per-row as order-of-magnitude placeholders rather than source-derived numbers, the same treatment given to several Genghis Khan and Saladin rows elsewhere in this dataset. tech_era_tier=1 for every row, matching Caesar and Alexander. resource_backing_tier varies 1-3 across the roster reflecting Hannibal's genuinely worsening resource situation over the war -- tier 2 for the freshly-arrived invasion force of 218-217 BC, tier 3 at Cannae (his largest, best-reinforced army of the war) and at Zama (home-soil mobilization, though a scratch army), tier 1 at Petelia (208 BC, the isolated Bruttium endgame). Net roster is 6 wins and 1 loss: undefeated in every included Italian battle, with the one loss being Zama itself, the war-deciding battle against Scipio Africanus -- a fair summary of Hannibal's actual reputation (tactically formidable, strategically unable to force Rome to terms, and beaten only once it mattered most).

Scope limited to major set-piece battles/sieges personally supreme-commanded during the Second Punic War (209-202 BC) with quantifiable troop-strength and casualty figures on both sides -- same personal-command and no-fabrication bars used for every general in this dataset. Excludes the Battle of the Great Plains (Campi Magni, 203 BC), the field battle that immediately followed the Battle of the Camps: both Polybius (Histories XIV.8-9) and Livy (Ab Urbe Condita XXX.8) narrate the battle in tactical detail (Scipio's double envelopment of the Celtiberian center, Syphax and Hasdrubal Gisco's escape) but neither gives any casualty figure, killed or captured, for either side -- the same no-fabrication bar applied to Alexander's Persian Gate and Genghis's Khalakhaljid Sands elsewhere in this dataset. Also excludes the Battle of Cirta (203 BC, fought by Scipio's legate Gaius Laelius and Masinissa while Scipio himself was besieging Utica) and the Battle against Vermina (202 BC, fought by Gnaeus Octavius after Zama while Scipio marched on Carthage) -- both well-attested with casualty figures but neither personally commanded by Scipio, the same subordinate-command exclusion applied to Genghis's Irtysh River/Parwan and Saladin's al-Babein elsewhere. Also excludes Scipio's earlier presence (not command) at Ticinus (218 BC, where as a young military tribune he saved his wounded father, already a row in Hannibal's roster with the father Publius Cornelius Scipio as opponent_general_id) and at Cannae (216 BC, survived the battle as a junior officer under his elders' command). Net roster is 5 rows, on the low end of this dataset's usual 8-15 range for the same structural reason as Zhukov's 6-battle roster and Hannibal's 7-battle roster: Scipio's independent-command career was short (7 years) and several of his other well-known engagements (Great Plains, Cirta, Vermina) fail either the no-fabrication or the personal-command bar rather than being a research shortfall. All 5 rows are wins; Scipio is undefeated in personal command, culminating in the battle that ended the Second Punic War against Hannibal himself.

Scope limited to battles where Subutai (Sube'etei) held personal supreme command or joint co-equal command with Jebe, applying this dataset's established 'personally supreme-commanded' bar (already used to exclude Genghis Khan's Irtysh River/Parwan, Saladin's al-Babein, Frederick's Kesselsdorf, Napoleon's Auerstedt, Grant's Corinth, and Zhukov's Stalingrad/Kursk/Bagration). Net roster is 5 rows -- Battle of Khunan (1222), Battle of Khankala (1222), Battle of the Kalka River (1223), Battle of Mohi (1241), Siege of Kaifeng (1232-33) -- the thinnest roster in this dataset alongside Scipio Africanus (5) and a deliberate research finding, not a shortcut: Subutai spent most of his 50-year career as a senior subordinate commander under Genghis Khan, then Ogedei, then Batu, and the great majority of his most famous campaigns fail either the personal-command bar or the no-fabricated-numbers bar on closer sourcing. Excluded on the personal-command bar (someone else held the specific battle's named field command, even though Subutai contributed forces or planning to the same campaign): the 1216-1219 Merkit pursuit campaign (Chem River) -- Christopher Atwood credits Jochi with supreme command, Subutai leading only a subordinate contingent, the same 'Irtysh River' pattern already excluded from Genghis Khan's own roster; the Siege of Kolomna (1238) -- Wikipedia's own battle-specific infobox names Burundai and Kulkan as commanders and does not list Subutai at all, despite secondary campaign-level summaries placing him with the invasion force, a materially weaker individual attribution than this dataset requires; the Battle of the Sit River (1238) -- field command held by Burundai; the Battle of Legnica (1241) -- commanded by princes Baidar and Kaidan on a separate front from Subutai's own column, with Subutai credited only with prior planning guidance to Baidar's detachment; the Siege of Nishapur (1221) -- commanded by Tolui, Subutai operating elsewhere in Persia/Azerbaijan by that point in the Khwarazmian pursuit; the Sack of Ryazan (1237) -- individual command attribution weaker than Kolomna's, most summaries crediting Batu directly. Also excluded on a genuine, unresolved command-attribution dispute rather than a clean subordinate-command case: the Battle of Sanfengshan (Feb 1232), the decisive field battle that destroyed the Jin's last army immediately before the Kaifeng row above -- Wikipedia's own battle-specific article credits Tolui as tactical planner (Ogedei present) and does not mention Subutai, while Subutai's own biographical literature (Gabriel's book-length framing especially) credits him as the tactical author; without a source giving Subutai direct, specific personal command the way the Yuan Shi does for Mohi below, this is treated as excludable per the same strict standard used for Zhukov's Stavka-coordinator battles -- flagged here since it is the closest call in this roster and a strong tactical case exists for including it. Also excluded, same reason: the Battle of Daohuigu (Nov 1230-Jan 1231), Subutai's one credible personal defeat candidate (a costly Mongol repulse at Tongguan Pass, 'more than 10,000 soldiers and tens of thousands of horses' lost in Mongol chronicles) -- command is split between Tolui's first phase and a second phase credited to Subutai, and the one hard casualty figure found is not clearly attributable to Subutai's specific phase rather than Tolui's; including it risked crediting or debiting Subutai for losses that may not be his. As a consequence this roster has no losses (5 wins), not because Subutai's real record was flawless -- Daohuigu is a real, well-documented personal setback in his career -- but because the one candidate defeat with real numbers failed this dataset's attribution-integrity bar specifically, the mirror image of how Zhukov's roster includes Operation Mars as a real loss precisely because that one is cleanly attributed. Excluded on the no-fabrication bar (real, notable engagements with no quantifiable troop-strength or casualty figure for one or both sides in any source found, the same bar used for Alexander's Persian Gate, Genghis's Khalakhaljid Sands, Saladin's Marj Ayyun, Hannibal's Nola battles, and Scipio's Great Plains): the Battle of the Irghiz River (1219, engagement broken off at nightfall before a real battle developed, no casualties in any source and an unresolved, wildly divergent troop-strength range depending on which of two disputed dates -- 1209 or 1219 -- a source assumes); the Battle of Sagim/Sagimi (1221, an earlier, less-documented Georgia engagement, only qualitatively 'massacred', no numbers); the Battle of Samara Bend (1223, Volga Bulgaria -- command itself is unresolved between Subutai, Jebe, and Jochi, and troop strength is flatly 'unknown' on both sides; one primary account suggests this may actually have been a rare Mongol defeat, but with no numbers to anchor a row either way); and the 1220 Jebe/Subutai pursuit of Muhammad II through Rayy, Qazvin, and Hamadan (a chevauchee of city-sacking, not a discrete two-sided pitched battle -- no troop count for the opposing side or a casualty figure for any single engagement survives, only qualitative destruction language for the sacked cities as a whole; the Kalka River row already captures this same reconnaissance-in-force campaign's culmination). era=Medieval and tech_era_tier=2 for every row, matching Genghis Khan and Saladin, the dataset's other Medieval-era generals -- Subutai's entire personal-command career fell within Genghis Khan's reign and the regencies/khanates of his immediate successors, the same stirrup-cavalry, pre-gunpowder-artillery technology basis (the Kaifeng row's Jin thunder-crash bombs were a defensive weapon used against the Mongols, not part of the Mongol army's own arsenal, so it does not change this general's own tech tier). resource_backing_tier is set per-row (2 for the 1222-1223 Caucasus/Kalka reconnaissance-in-force, cut off from home-base resupply and operating on what the force could forage; 4 for Mohi, part of the empire-scale western campaign under Ogedei's direct authorization; 5 for Kaifeng, the converged main imperial siege army under the reigning Great Khan's direct command before Subutai assumed sole authority) -- same per-row approach as Frederick, Napoleon, and Grant elsewhere in this dataset. Net record is 5 wins, 0 losses (see the Daohuigu exclusion above for why -- not a claim of an undefeated career, a data-attribution-integrity limitation of this specific roster).

Scope limited to battles/sieges Tokugawa personally commanded (sole command, or, for allied battles, command of a genuinely distinct sub-force with separately attributable results) with quantifiable troop-strength AND casualty figures on both sides. Six rows: Anegawa (1570), Mikatagahara (1573), Siege of Takatenjin (1581), Nagakute (1584), Sekigahara (1600), Tennoji/Summer Siege of Osaka (1615). Notably excludes the Battle of Nagashino (1575), despite Tokugawa being named among its commanders: sources state Oda Nobunaga 'took command of the entire army' on arrival, with the decisive palisade/ arquebus-volley plan and flanking maneuver both attributed to Nobunaga and Tokugawa reduced to a named subordinate on the line -- the same personal-command bar already used to exclude Saladin's al-Babein (Shirkuh in overall command) and Zhukov's Stalingrad/ Kursk (Zhukov as Stavka coordinator, not front commander) elsewhere in this dataset. Also excludes the broader Komaki standoff (1584, months of fortified maneuver with no single quantifiable pitched-battle casualty figure -- Nagakute, the one attributable clash within that campaign, is included separately), the Winter Campaign of the Siege of Osaka (1614, clear troop strength but no source found quantifies campaign casualties), and three battles with clear personal command but no quantifiable casualty figures found in any source (Azukizaka 1564, the 1582 Wakamiko/Tensho-Jingo War campaign, and the 1585 First Siege of Ueda Castle, the last of which also has disputed command attribution -- Okubo Tadayo/Torii Mototada may have held actual field command rather than Tokugawa personally). Everything before the 1570 Anegawa row (Ieyasu's Imagawa-vassal period, including the 1560 Okehazama campaign where he commanded only a supply/vanguard detachment under Imagawa Yoshimoto) is excluded on the same not-yet-independent-command grounds used for Scipio's excluded junior-officer service under his father. tech_era_tier is set to 3 (gunpowder-era: matchlock arquebuses and cannon in regular use by the 1570s in Japan) rather than the 2 used for this dataset's other Medieval-era generals (Genghis Khan, Saladin, Subutai) -- a deliberate divergence: era='Medieval' here follows this project's SCOPE.md roster bucketing, but tech_era_tier is judged on the actual military technology in use at the battle, independent of the era-cohort label, and Sengoku-period Japan's gunpowder warfare is technologically closer to Frederick the Great's Early Modern tier-3 battles than to Mongol-era horse-archer warfare.

Scope covers 12 battles where Washington held personal, on-the-field command, spanning the French and Indian War (Jumonville Glen and Fort Necessity, 1754, as a 22-year-old Virginia Regiment colonel) and the American Revolution (Harlem Heights through Yorktown, 1776-81, as Continental Army commander-in-chief) -- a 27-year gap between the two wars during which no personally-commanded engagement with quantifiable figures was found (Braddock's 1755 defeat at the Monongahela doesn't count: Washington was an unpaid aide with no chain-of-command authority, not the commander; 1756-58 frontier command produced no documented combat contact). Excluded from the Revolutionary War roster on the same personal-command bar used elsewhere in this dataset: Long Island, Kip's Bay, and Fort Washington/Fort Lee (Putnam, Stirling, Sullivan, Greene, and Magaw ran the actual fighting while Washington observed, arrived too late, or was rebuffed at a remove), Stony Point and Springfield (Wayne and Greene commanded while Washington set strategy from a distance), and Paoli/the Battle of the Clouds (Washington absent, or no real engagement occurred). White Plains and Monmouth are qualified inclusions -- Washington personally directed the overall army-level plan even though a subordinate ran a specific phase (Chatterton's Hill at White Plains; Charles Lee's opening vanguard action at Monmouth, before Washington relieved him mid-battle) -- the same standard already used for Grant's Overland Campaign rows. Yorktown combines American and French troop/casualty figures into one field under Washington's protocol-supreme command (confirmed directly by Rochambeau's own memoir), the same multi-force-combination treatment already used for Alesia and Zhukov's Vistula-Oder Offensive; operational execution nonetheless stayed split by nationality (Redoubt 10 American, Redoubt 9 French), so this is siege-level and diplomatic-protocol command rather than Washington personally leading troops under fire the way he did at Trenton or Princeton. tech_era_tier=3 for every row, matching Frederick the Great's contemporaneous linear-gunpowder-warfare tier (the French and Indian War and the Seven Years' War are the same global conflict, 1754/56-1763). Real record: 5 wins (Jumonville Glen, Harlem Heights, Trenton, Princeton, Yorktown), 3 losses (Fort Necessity, Brandywine, Germantown), 2 draws (Assunpink Creek, Monmouth), 1 loss/withdrawal (White Plains), plus a minor defensive win at Whitemarsh -- personal command clusters overwhelmingly around moments of institutional crisis (a raw militia colonel signing a French 'assassination' accusation at Fort Necessity, an army facing mass enlistment expiration at Trenton, a supply system collapsing toward 'this Army might dissolve' around Germantown/Whitemarsh), not around periods of strength.

19 rows -- above this dataset's usual 8-15 target, a deliberate deviation rather than a forced round number: Wellington's ~12-year documented independent-command career (India 1803; the Peninsular War 1808-1814; the Hundred Days 1815) is unusually comprehensively sourced by name-brand historians (Oman's 7-volume History of the Peninsular War covers nearly every engagement in detail) with essentially no battles failing the no-fabrication bar, the opposite problem from Hannibal/Scipio/Subutai/Zhukov's under-target rosters elsewhere in this dataset. Cutting battles that clearly clear both the personal-command and no-fabrication bars purely to hit a round number would repeat the mistake this dataset's own Phase 2 notes explicitly avoided in the other direction (padding thin rosters to hit a count) -- so all 19 are kept, flagged here for Phase 7's eventual sanity-pass re-run. Includes the 1803 India campaign (Assaye, Argaon), fought under the Wellesley name six years before the Peninsular War and the dukedom -- included as a scope call matching Napoleon's Montenotte precedent (a general's first independent command, well-sourced, personally led). Command-attribution calls follow this dataset's established 'personally directed the overall plan counts even when a subordinate ran a specific phase' standard (Vimeiro's Burrard-outranks-but-doesn't-intervene case) and its mirror, the personal-command bar excluding parallel subordinate-led actions (San Sebastián, run independently by Thomas Graham while Wellington fought Sorauren simultaneously -- same treatment as Napoleon's Auerstedt exclusion from Jena). Talavera (1809) isolates Wellesley's own British force from Cuesta's separate Spanish command (no formal subordination found, unlike Yorktown), while Vitoria (1813) combines the full multinational Allied total since Spanish divisions were genuinely integrated into his order of battle by then -- two structurally similar 'allied force present' situations resolved oppositely based on the actual command relationship each time, not a fixed rule. Waterloo isolates Wellington's Anglo-allied force from Blücher's Prussians for the same no-subordination reason as Talavera; its enemy_troop_strength/enemy_casualties are set to match napoleon-waterloo-1815's own-side figures exactly, while that existing Napoleon row's enemy figures remain the combined Anglo+Prussian total -- a documented, intentional asymmetry between the two generals' rows for the same battle, not a data inconsistency. Net record is 18 wins (5 Rout-level: Argaon, Salamanca, Vitoria, Waterloo, and effectively Assaye by casualty ratio though labeled Strategic) / 1 loss (Burgos, his clearest field failure, included for an honest record). tech_era_tier=4 matches Napoleon and Grant's rows throughout, including the two 1803 India battles, since the schema tracks absolute technology level (flintlock muskets, smoothbore cannon, animal-powered logistics) rather than era-cohort label, and India in 1803 was contemporaneous with -- not behind -- the same global weapons generation.

Scope covers 14 rows: Lee's personal, independent field command of the Army of Northern Virginia from taking over on June 1, 1862 (first battle Gaines's Mill, June 27) through the surrender at Appomattox (April 9, 1865). Excludes his pre-1862 career (a staff/engineering officer in the Mexican-American War, superintendent of West Point, and briefly a field commander of a minor, unsuccessful 1861 western Virginia campaign at Cheat Mountain that never rises to a usable battle-level row) under the same personal-independent-command bar used for every other general on this roster. Seven of the fourteen rows (Wilderness, Spotsylvania, Cold Harbor, the Crater, Globe Tavern, Third Petersburg, Appomattox) mirror existing grant-*-1864/1865 rows -- own/enemy strength and casualty fields swapped so both generals' rows agree on the same battles, the same treatment already used for the Napoleon/Wellington Waterloo pair and the Hannibal/Scipio Zama pair. The Second Battle of Petersburg (June 1864) is deliberately excluded from this mirrored set even though it sits chronologically inside it: per Grant's own row for that battle, the defending garrison was commanded solely by P.G.T. Beauregard, with Lee's army arriving from the Overland Campaign only as the assaults were ending, the same subordinate-command exclusion bar used elsewhere in this dataset (see lee-crater-1864's notes for the full reasoning). resource_backing_tier is set per-row on a deliberately declining curve -- 3 through Gettysburg (July 1863, the Army of Northern Virginia's organizational and manpower peak), 2 through the 1864 Overland Campaign and the Crater/Globe Tavern phase of the Petersburg siege (a real, shrinking, irreplaceable manpower pool against an opponent who could replace losses), and 1 for the final two 1865 rows (the army starving and disintegrating through desertion in the war's last weeks) -- the intentional mirror-image of Grant's own rising 2-through-5 resource curve on the same roster, since the two sides' real wartime mobilization trajectories moved in opposite directions. tech_era_tier is flat 4 across all rows, matching Grant's row (same conflict, same technology). political_constraint_flag is true for Antietam and Gettysburg (both invasions had explicit political objectives -- foreign recognition, Northern peace-movement pressure) and true for every 1864 row from the Wilderness through Third Petersburg (Jefferson Davis's standing order to hold Richmond/Petersburg at essentially any cost, a different and longer-lived constraint than the election-cycle pressure that drives Grant's own flag on the same mirrored rows, documented per-row); false again at Appomattox once the Confederate government had already fled the capital and Lee's surrender decision was his own military judgment. Net record is 6 wins (2 Rout-level: Second Bull Run, the Crater) / 6 losses (1 Rout-level: Appomattox) / 2 draws (Wilderness, Spotsylvania) -- an unusually well-balanced record for this dataset's roster, reflecting Lee's real historiographical reputation as a general who dominated the battlefield for most of his tenure and still lost the war, the same 'brilliant on the field, lost the war' pattern PLAN.md's Squander Index is specifically designed to capture.
